The previous post in this series covered RAG (or "rules of grammar"). This post covers the seven context window components, strategies for managing them, how they fail, and a real token budget.
GPT-3 was released in 2020 and was the largest language model at the time at 200 billion parameters. It was impressive, but also bugged out wildly when given the wrong prompts. "Predicting next word sequences" is a task that the new generation of language models are good at, but for any more complex tasks, it's not so clear what to do.
The new language models (including GPT-4, which is reportedly 200 billion parameters) are safe to use in most cases, but only when we use them responsibly. One way to use them irresponsibly is to take a prompt that you think is safe, and then modify it slightly, swapping "summarize" for "explain briefly", adding "step by step", rearranging words, or telling the model to roleplay as a character with no safety guidelines. Any of these could change the GPT-3 output from incoherent to useful to harmful.
Early context windows were about 4 thousand tokens, and now they're around 200 thousand tokens. Andrej Karpathy called context engineering "the delicate art and science of filling the context window with just the right information for the next step".
For example, a diabetes management coaching agent that I built with LangGraph used 5 agent prompts to interact with the user. Each of these prompts pulled in several graphs which were then pulled into the model as a single prompt:
The system prompt is one of the seven components that fills the context window. It usually contains information about the system, like the prompt name or how to contact the agent. Here's an example of one of the seven components:
The user prompt is a prompt that contains information about the current user who is interacting with the agent. It might contain the user's name, age, or the problem they need help with.
The agent prompt is a prompt that contains information about the agent who is interacting with the user. It might contain the agent's name or their job title.
The data prompt is a prompt that contains information about the data that will be used by the agent. It might contain the name of the database or the type of data that will be extracted.
The format prompt is a prompt that contains information about the format that the data will be returned in. It might contain the name of the format or the type of data that will be returned.
The RAG prompt is a prompt that contains information about the grammar rules that will be used by the agent. It might contain the name of the RAG file or the type of grammar that will be used.
The token budget is how many tokens you have to fill the prompt. The engineer, or someone on the team, should set the budget. Look at the example prompts above and figure out how many tokens are in each prompt. How many tokens do you have left for the remaining prompt?

Context engineering is a term we use at Manus for the process of building agents that work with massive context windows, for example in triage systems that must consider a patient's entire medical history. There are a few different frontiers of context engineering right now:
- There’s the conventional “cut and paste from legal docs / compliance docs / external resources” approach, which can inflate context windows to several thousand tokens, but doesn’t require structural understanding
- There’s the more sophisticated approach of using self-describing nested objects, which is amenable to ~200-300 tokens
- There’s the true “context” approach, which involves modeling the agent’s workflow and loading only what’s needed, like in Claude Code
- There’s the very sophisticated approach of dynamically loading and removing tools, which is what we do at Manus
When you get into the multiple-thousand-token range, things get exponentially more expensive. Claude Code, which has 300+ conversation tools, is a good case study for this dynamic, where the cost of retrieving a tool doubles with every nested call. A moderately complex schema with nested objects, descriptions and enums can consume 300+ tokens.
What’s most remarkable is that Claude Code is a fairly simple agent — the average number of conversation tools is in the 4-6 range, not 40, and the agent’s biggest expense is not its context window but the logical consistency between tools, inasmuch as it needs to deduce how best to use them all together.
Despite the author’s best efforts, Claude Code loads its conversation tools dynamically, at each turn, and that has the unfortunate side effect of breaking KV-cache, which is Manus’s preferred cache strategy. Given that Manus’s agents have dozens of tools, the math on cache invalidation probably dominates.
The dynamic nature of Claude Code also means that we can’t easily use the sort of explicit cache control that’s offered by Anthropic and OpenAI, where we can choose to only cache certain parts of the conversation. Toggling features like web search also invalidates the system cache, which is why those tend to be uncached.
What’s the fundamental issue here? Why is KV-cache so sensitive to dynamic? The author imagines it has to do with JSON key ordering instability in certain languages (like Swift and Go), which can silently affect caches.
The following is a solution that Manus uses to work around this issue:
- In our state block, we report the current turn, the conversation phase, the time of day, and which tools were already called
- In the state block, we can then use a state machine to ensure that nothing superfluous is included in the cache
- This also has the benefit of capping the state block to 50-100 tokens
- This approach allows us to cache up to 10, but realistically 300% of our state block, which is a nice compromise
One advantage of this KV-cache-based approach is that it’s very simple. Remember that the state block is only 50-100 tokens, and the "extra context" block is another ~200 tokens. That means that the state block is 10% of the entire context window. It also means that we can’t stash that much in the KV-cache, so we’d run up against an upper limit pretty quickly.
What’s more, we’re working with a state block that’s already structured — the state block, which is 50-100 tokens, is actually broken into XML-tagged sections. So at a glance, we can get an idea of how much work is required to evaluate the context. In the case of the pump troubleshooting example, the engine will load only those lines that pertain to Type 1 and not the entire section, and thanks to our XML tagging, the model can easily distinguish between the two.
The example above illustrates how the engine can perform extremely targeted cache operations: instead of caching the entire state block, which would be roughly 200+ tokens, we can cache only relevant sections, like the current turn, conversation phase, time of day and tools that were already called, which is about 10% of the state block.
By contrast, a state block-based cache means we would have to cache a lot more information. From a 200-token state block, we might cache only 100 tokens, which is expensive, or we might cache all 200, but that’s also expensive.
What would it look like if we used a state block to cache, given that the state block is just 50-100 tokens?
- If we tried to cache only 100 tokens, we’d be working with a 10-200% cache
- If we tried to cache all 200 tokens, we’d be working with a 50-100% cache
That’s too much or not enough, depending on what you’re trying to do.
It’s hard to imagine a circumstance where we would want to cache the state block in its entirety. Instead, our approach is to cache a portion of the state block, and because we have some structure to our conversation state, we can say only the relevant lines need to be cached. In the previous pump troubleshooting example, we can eliminate the entire Type 2 section, which should be enough for our model to make a decision.
This approach is more efficient because we’re dealing with a fixed-size state block, but it still has some drawbacks: a state block cache isn’t going to work very well with agents that spawn subagents, and it’s also not very well suited to agents that have 70+ tools to synthesize research papers and technical posts.
Still, what we’re seeing is a phenomenon that’s not exclusive to agents but true of all models. The state block cache means the agent has to remember only a fraction of the entire conversation, which is great for performance and memory but not so good for larger-scale inference. In the example above, a condition filter means a Type 2 patient will never see Type 1 insulin pump troubleshooting guides, without the patient or model specifying that constraint.
Still, the state block cache can be a great solution for agents that work with fixed, predictable context windows. In Part 4 of this series, we’ll examine the use case of the filesystem as the agent’s working memory.

Context engineering strategies for LLM agents
Context engineering is a critical part of building successful LLM agents. The size of the conversational context that an agent can handle is especially important for full-stack applications, where the LLM has to manage multiple threads.
The Manus platform has developed a few techniques that I’ll briefly cover here. I’ll also share some of the research motivations behind them. These strategies can be broadly categorized into the four strategies that LangChain’s framework has named.
How to handle context
My goal is to start compacting in the 80-90% range, before 95%. In practice summarization applies to conversations beyond ~15 turns. We’re thinking about how to compact even longer conversations to cut our raw context cost by 50%. This would put us in the 50-80% range, leaving us with room to scale.
The simplest way to compress the incoming context is to truncate it. However, the LLM often degrades when you take this approach, because it’s relying on that context to provide guidance. To mitigate this, our first strategy is to scale the context structure.
Context scaling
Our first strategy is to scale the context structure. We trim the context tree and only pass down the latest conversation, rather than the entire conversation history. This doesn’t change the message volume but does free up some of the node capacity.
The second strategy is to convert the conversation history into a more abstract representation. The idea here is to move away from “I think we talked about money” to “the conversation is about money.”
The Manus agent relies on a soft knowledge base. It has a metadata layer that provides some basic guidance, but it primarily relies on the agent’s knowledge base for context.
The agent’s knowledge base is comprised of semi-structured documents. As the conversation progresses, the agent continually updates its knowledge base with more information. This is useful because it allows the agent to maintain references to context over long conversations.
The agent’s knowledge base has a direct impact on the LLM’s performance. The agent’s knowledge base is also its own primary context source.
This strategy also prevents LLM degradation from the conversation history being removed from the conversation thread. In other words, the LLM doesn’t have to rely on context to maintain its own understanding.
Query rewriter
The third strategy is to rewrite the user’s message into a self-contained retrieval query before searching. This approach gives the agent more control over the entire search process, rather than just selecting the response out of the LLM’s output.
The Manus agent has a query rewriter built in. The rewriter infers “post-meal readings” from the last 3 turns. It also adds the patient’s diagnosis and medication context, producing a query that hits relevant documents.
This query is much more effective than the original message, which has almost zero retrieval value due the lack of context for the patient’s condition or medications.
Summarize to degrade gracefully
The final strategy is to treat the LLM like a black box and apply “context engineering” directly to the LLM’s output. We can combine summarization with our existing structures to create a more fluid user experience.
The first strategy is to compact the conversation’s previous turns. This removes the “back and forth” that we expect users to answer in their own words.
Our summarization tier fires only when compaction cannot get below 85% capacity. Our second strategy is to retain the last 50 turns. We must retain some context, because the agent’s knowledge base relies on it.
A summary with context has a better chance of staying relevant to the user. The output gate sees only the agent’s response and a scope-checking prompt. The input gate sees only the latest user message and a short classification prompt.
Sub-agents return a condensed summary (13, 2, 3 tokens) to the lead agent. This means the agent doesn’t have to worry about dropping any conversation thread. Any new turn is just added to the active conversation threads.
The Manus team has let our agents maintain a file during complex tasks. The agents write and re-read their plan, which is an internal structure that helps to counter the “lost-in-the-middle” problem across ~50 average tool calls.
Our fourth strategy is to fill gaps in the conversation with the agent’s own understanding of the conversation. To do this, we use our knowledge base, the agent’s internal representation of the conversation.
The third strategy is to use the agent’s knowledge base as the source of the conversation’s current state. This allows us to maintain a conversation state as an internal structure that we can “re-construct” from the conversation history.
We’re able to keep our conversation’s state essentially as a “cache.” The knowledge base is an internal structure that contains a conversation state that we can “re-construct” from the conversation history.
The fourth strategy is to use the agent’s knowledge base as the source of the conversation’s current state. This allows us to maintain a conversation state as an internal structure that we can “re-construct” from the conversation history.
Compaction to degrade gracefully
Our first strategy is to make sure the LLM always sees roughly the same information it’s expecting. We reduce the current user message and previous response to something like “thanks” or “ok sounds good.” This approach removes “back and forth” that we expect users to answer in their own words.
We have one layer with several “spokes” that handle different aspects of the conversation. The “spokes” are the sub-agents that do the actual work. The lead agent coordinates them.

The second strategy is to create a more abstract representation of the context. We build this structure into our agent. This means the agent can “look back” at any conversation turn. It also allows us to “look ahead” at the conversation thread.

HuggingFace’s CodeAgent framework is great at isolating token-heavy objects into sandbox environments, keeping only references in the main context. Recurrent research into context compression has found that compressing instructions and context simultaneously degrades responses.
Our research has found that decomposing a complex task into sub-stages improves the LLM’s accuracy. Researchers at RAG-MC have found that isolating tasks into sub-agents helps to improve the agent’s performance.
There’s another interesting twist to this research. RAG-MC found that performance improves when you remove the context of sub-agents once they’ve finished their tasks. This context cleanup strategy is the key to making this approach work.
The team at Manus has been able to make their agent more context-aware by combining summarization with their existing structures. They’ve found that this approach creates a more fluid user experience.
The LangChain team has developed a framework that names the four strategies in this article. The team at RAG-MC has found that their agent’s performance improves when they isolate the task context into sub-agents.
The team at OpenAI has found that production SDKs from both OpenAI and Anthropic trim out text in atomic turn groups. The HuggingFace team’s “CodeAgent” framework is great at isolating token-heavy objects into sandbox environments.
The RAG-MC paper saw tool selection accuracy rise from 13. 15% to 43. 15% compared to exposing all tools at once. The Manus team developed a strategy that uses their agent’s knowledge base as the source of the conversation’s current state.

Context failure modes
By Anthropic
This week, we’ve been digging into some of our models’ context failure modes. Here are some of the most interesting ones we’ve found so far.
The lost-in-the-middle finding (Liu et al., 2023)
Last week, we documented a consistent U-shaped curve across models and settings: performance degrades significantly when relevant information sits in the middle of long contexts versus the beginning or end. We found a few mechanisms driving this, but are still digging into the root cause. These two examples show the same basic pattern:
The agent wrote "TEA" into its goals scratchpad
This agent hallucinated an item called "TEA". It spent hundreds of actions trying to find it, which doesn’t exist in the game. It’s hard to say how this happened for sure, but it seems like the agent’s attention budget is overwhelmingly focused on the Pokemon’s name at the end, and not the items it has in the middle. This item was nowhere in the original context, so it must’ve been entirely synthesized, but the agent spent a lot of energy trying to dig up the nonexistent item.
This agent developed a "black-out strategy": intentionally fainting all its Pokemon to teleport. This is a clever strategy, but the agent only ever teleports back to the first place it fainted. You can see this here: the agent is fainting only its first two Pokemon, and never teleporting beyond the first island.
A fetch tool clash
Here’s a more subtle failure mode we found recently. Our Pokemon-playing agent has a tool that can fetch a Pokemon’s hidden stats, which are sometimes not directly visible.
The agent sometimes calls the tool anyway, wasting a round-trip to fetch data already in the prompt. This is because the agent’s instruction is in the prompt section, and the tool definition is in the Python code.
This is easy to miss because the instruction is in the prompt section, and the tool definition is in Python code. The agent sometimes calls the tool anyway, wasting a round-trip to fetch data already in the prompt.
Beyond ~100, 100 tokens, we’ve also noticed our agents tend to repeat actions from history over synthesizing novel plans. This isn’t surprising: at 100, 100, 100 tokens, the model’s attention budget is spread across billions of pair interactions, and critical information gets drowned out. We’re seeing a similar effect with our other tasks, where agents start repeating the same actions over and over once they go beyond ~100, 100, 100 tokens.
The system prompt says "When READING information you already have in the patient context above, use it directly, do not re-fetch with .". But the fetch tool is still available as a callable tool, contradicting the instruction.
Chroma attributes the mechanism behind context distraction to the $O(n^2)$ pairwise token relationships in self-attention, which means the model’s attention budget is spread across billions of pair interactions.
What are good agents good for?How good are large language models?
Google DeepMind’s Gemini 2.100 technical report documents a similar context poisoning finding, where the model simply pays no attention to the part of the context that’s relevant for making good recommendations.
We’re seeing similar trends with our agents, where they sometimes don’t pay attention to the important parts of the context, and instead default to what they learned by previous exposure to similar contexts.
In previous work, we’ve found agents can perform much more reliably when provided with a single, short instruction that gets repeated in the context. Our latest experiments follow a similar pattern: by repeating our instructions, we get much higher accuracy and lower error.
The mechanism behind the context distraction we’re seeing looks very similar to the context poisoning described in our recent research. How much context is enough?We’ve found that with anything beyond ~100, 100, 100 tokens, the model’s attention budget is spread across billions of pair interactions, and critical information starts getting drowned out.
A solid guiding principle we’re using: find the smallest set of high-signal tokens that maximize the likelihood of your desired outcome.
You can apply this same rule to the agent’s instructions: instead of a long passage of text, use a single instruction and repeat it to increase the likelihood the agent will notice it.

Manus just reported a 10× cost difference: $0.3/MTok cached vs $3/MTok uncached on Claude Sonnet. The problem is a KV-cache violation: the volatile block of state changes every turn with new turn count, new timestamp and new tool history so the prompt prepended with volatile state invalidates the cache every turn.
Initially we thought the solution would be a KV-cache violation, only to find that in case 120 the access rights on the KV-cache are only to be able to read the state, not to write to it. The write right is held by the KV-module which updates the KV-cache with the block of state. There is no way to prevent the KV-module from writing to the KV-cache.
By trying to limit the reading from the KV-cache to only the user profile we’ve found that the system prompt ranges from ~2,0KM to ~4,0 KM depending on the session maturity. The user profile of the patient is injected in the system prompt on every turn and acts as a KV-read limit. By removing the tool entirely we’ve fixed the redundant fetches.
The conversation window is char-budgeted at 120.0K characters and the system prompt is built of a combination of the following:
- the system prompt (ranges from ~2,0 KM to ~4,0 KM depending on the session maturity)
- the patient profile
- the user profile
- the previous turn context
- the tool instructions
By removing the tool we’ve found that the KV-cache violation initially spotted was a KV-cache violation, but the problem was actually a KV-read violation (a KV-cache violation would cause a 10× cost difference). By removing the tool and thus the KV-read violation we’ve made the agent more confident in referencing the profile data from the prompt.
We’ve also found that the conversation window holds a maximum of 6 turns and that the patient profile also exists as a callable tool. It is injected into the system prompt on every turn. Context-Bench (and Letta Context-Bench) are benchmarks for evaluating your context engineering capability. They are about asking your coding agent to retrieve the right context from 66 real repositories across 8 languages. We are actually looking at two aspects:
- The ability of your coding agent to retrieve specific text fragments within a large body of text
- The ability of your engineering team to build out your coding agent using real repositories
Both are very important to have. The former tests whether you have a good architecture for your agent, the latter test whether you have a good engineering team to build your agent. It is worth checking your metrics here.
Here is how I did it:
- I first trained a single model on the 66 repositories (Code: https://github.com/desistare/ContextBench)
- I got a 74.0% accuracy for $24.5

The claim that we “need to worry about costs at the context level” is true, but it’s not the whole story.
We should also worry about costs at the output level.
This story is true of any time you have a choice between competing paradigms where:
1) The total expense of each paradigm is linear in the cost of one particular subcomponent
(Note that this is true for both the expressivity regime of Claude and the expressivity regime of GPT.)
And
1) The performance of each paradigm is sub-linear in the cost of that subcomponent
So there are at least two things we can do:
a) We can optimize the cost of that subcomponent, which will improve the total expense
b) We can increase the performance of that subcomponent, which will improve the total performance
The relative advantage of each approach depends on the shape of the curve. Suppose that’s true here:
a) If the subcomponent is 10% of the cost, a 10% optimization in that subcomponent can reduce the total expense by 10%.
b) If the subcomponent is 10% of the performance, a 10% improvement in that subcomponent can improve the total performance by 10%.
So a 10% improvement in the subcomponent is worth a 10% reduction in the subcomponent.
Now suppose that:
a) The subcomponent is 10% of the expense, and a 10% improvement in that subcomponent can reduce the total expense by 10%.
b) The subcomponent is 50% of the performance, and a 10% improvement in that subcomponent can improve the total performance by 50%.
Now a 10% improvement in the subcomponent is worth a 50% reduction in the subcomponent.
If you have an application where the output tokens outnumber the input tokens by roughly 100:1, then at scale the input-side optimization will matter more than the output-side optimization. The issue isn’t the absolute costs, but the relative costs.
I have a lot of faith in the ability of humans to optimize near-term costs. I’m less optimistic about our ability to optimize long-term costs. (I would say that’s a feature of our brains, but I don’t know enough to make that claim.)
In this particular case, we can’t just direct our attention toward optimizing the context. We also need to worry about the output. When I look at this problem, I see two viable strategies:
- Compress proactively at 80-90% of context capacity, instead of compressing reactively at 95%. Yes, this may increase the cost of the context, but the context still dominates.
- Compress reactively, but look for ways to reduce the cost of both the output and the context. We need to squeeze that cost-volume-optimization curve.
